title: The Intel 4004 and the Birth of the Microprocessor (1971)
explainer: Embedded systems became possible as a mass-market category once an entire CPU could fit on one chip. The Intel 4004, released in November 1971 and originally designed for a Busicom calculator, is generally credited as the first commercially produced microprocessor, built by a team including Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, and Stan Mazor. That single-chip design is the direct ancestor of the microcontrollers this lesson's real-time code targets.

title: Liu and Layland's Rate-Monotonic Scheduling Theorem (1973)
explainer: Real-time systems need a provable guarantee that every periodic task meets its deadline, not just good average performance. Liu and Layland's 1973 paper supplied the first such guarantee: giving fixed priority to whichever task repeats most often (rate-monotonic scheduling) is provably optimal among fixed-priority schemes, and a task set is guaranteed schedulable if its total CPU utilization stays under a computable bound (about 0.83 for two tasks, falling toward ln 2, roughly 0.69, as the task count grows). This is why real-time operating systems can mathematically certify that deadlines will never be missed, rather than just hoping.
